subject: Creativity
title: Satire: Comedy That Bites Back
description: A micro-lesson that makes Satire: Comedy That Bites Back usable.

hook.text: Jonathan Swift proposed eating Irish babies to solve famine.

buildup.text: Satire uses humor, irony, and exaggeration to criticize society, politics, or human nature.

discovery.text: The best satire is indistinguishable from reality — which is why The Onion's headlines are sometimes reported as real.

twist.text: Dictators fear satire more than journalism. Charlie Hebdo, South Park, and political cartoonists face real threats.

climax.text: Studies show satirical news (Daily Show, Last Week Tonight) produces better-informed viewers than traditional news.

punchline.text: Satire is the sharpest criticism wrapped in the softest packaging.

quiz.question: Why do dictators fear satire more than journalism?
options: Comedy makes criticism more memorable and harder to suppress

details.summary: Satire uses humor to criticize institutions, power, and social norms. Unlike pure comedy, satire has a target and a purpose. From Jonathan Swift's modest proposals to modern late-night television, satire weaponizes laughter to expose hypocrisy.
details.whyItMatters: Satire has driven political change and social awareness throughout history. It remains one of the few tools that can challenge power structures while maintaining broad popular appeal.
takeaways: Satire targets specific institutions, people, or social norms
Effective satire requires deep knowledge of what it mocks
The best satire is funny even to those who disagree with its message

faq.question: What makes satire different from just being mean?
faq.answer: Satire punches up at power and institutions, not down at individuals. It uses exaggeration and irony to reveal truths rather than simply attacking. The intent is to provoke thought and change, not just to insult.

faq.question: Can satire actually change anything?
faq.answer: History shows satire can shift public opinion and hold power accountable. Shows like Saturday Night Live and publications like The Onion have influenced political discourse, though measuring direct policy impact is difficult.
